extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for recognizing, creating, and using flat versus round fictional characters: definitions, characteristic traits, examples, and how a character can move from flat toward round. Useful for writers working on characterization and story function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters created to represent a specific idea or quality; “immediately recognizable and can usually be represented by a single sentence,” who want one thing and serve a limited purpose in the story (E. M. Forster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters: lack depth or development; support the main character or other characters; often maintain the characteristics or familiar traits of a stereotype (e.g., the jilted bride); maintain one perspective or viewpoint; help create atmosphere, mood, or comedy; are vivid but simple; are predictable in behavior; are easily recognizable and remembered for those characteristics. Examples given: Miss Havisham (Great Expectations), Sykes (Oliver Twist), Benvolio (Romeo and Juliet), sitcom archetypes like the clueless parent or Newman (Seinfeld). Use flat characters when you need a clear, single-purpose figure to represent an idea or to support story function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters sufficiently complex “to be able to surprise the reader without losing credibility” (Forster) — realistically drawn figures with multiple aspects to their personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters: appear human with multiple aspects; let readers know what they are thinking; can surprise the reader; are convincing and rich in character with both flaws and qualities; have the potential to change and develop throughout the story; desire something; experience conflict and therefore undergo character development; may be likable or despicable. Round characters invite readers to see the world as they see it. Examples: Hamlet, Huck Finn, Anna Karenina, Mrs. Dalloway, Achilles, Captain Ahab, Lady Macbeth. Use rounding to deepen emotional investment and to provide believable change over the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition between flat and round (developmental guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters can move toward being round when they take on multiple aspects or when a realistic character 'defects' from stereotype — the flat persona 'curves towards the rounded character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a flat character acquires additional traits, perspectives, inner life, or conflicts, they may become rounded; conversely, losing traits can simplify a character. This is both a descriptive diagnostic (to identify when a character is one or the other) and a prescriptive tool for writers who wish to deepen a character over the course of a story.
